questions.question: What is essential for resource development to contribute to overall development?
options: The availability of resources alone is enough.
The presence of foreign invaders and their governance.
Only human resources can contribute to development.
questions.explanation: Resources contribute to development only when accompanied by appropriate technological development and institutional changes.
option_feedback: Availability alone is not enough; many resource-rich regions remain undeveloped.
Colonisers exploited resources; this did not develop the colonies.
Natural resources, technology and institutions all matter.

questions.question: Name three states having black soil and the crop which is mainly grown in it.

questions.question: What type of soil is found in the river deltas of the eastern coast? Give three main features of this type of soil.
answer_steps: Alluvial soil is found in the deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
It consists of sand, silt and clay, and is very fertile, with adequate potash, phosphoric acid and lime.
It is ideal for paddy, sugarcane, wheat, cereals and pulses, so these areas are intensively cultivated and densely populated.

questions.question: What steps can be taken to control soil erosion in the hilly areas?
answer_steps: Contour ploughing: ploughing along the contour lines slows the flow of water down the slopes.
Terrace cultivation: steps cut on the slopes check erosion, as in the western and central Himalayas.
Afforestation and controlled grazing; strip cropping and rows of trees reduce the force of water and wind.

questions.question: What are the biotic and abiotic resources? Give some examples.
answer_steps: Biotic resources are obtained from the biosphere and have life.
Examples: human beings, flora and fauna, fisheries and livestock.
Abiotic resources are composed of non-living things, for example rocks and metals.

questions.question: Explain the land use pattern in India and why the land under forest has not increased much since 1960-61.
answer_steps: Land use depends on physical factors (relief, climate, soil) and human factors (population, technology, culture); India's area is 3.28 million sq km, with land use data for about 93 per cent.

Land is classed as forests, land not available for cultivation, other uncultivated land, fallow land and net sown area; net sown area is over 80 per cent in Punjab and Haryana but under 10 per cent in Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Manipur and Andaman and Nicobar.
Land under permanent pasture has fallen, and land under non-agricultural uses has grown with cities and industries.
Forest cover has not increased much and remains far below the 33 per cent recommended by the National Forest Policy (1952).

Reasons: the growing population needs land for farming, housing, industries, roads and mining (as in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, MP and Odisha), and large development projects; so forests keep being cleared even as afforestation goes on.

questions.question: How have technical and economic development led to more consumption of resources?
answer_steps: New technology made it possible to extract and use resources such as minerals, fossil fuels and water on a large scale.
Industrialisation and mass production created demand for ever more raw materials and energy.
Rising incomes increased consumption of goods, vehicles and electricity, using up resources faster.
Colonisers with better technology exploited the resources of colonies; today resources gather in a few hands, dividing society into haves and have-nots.
This indiscriminate use has caused depletion, global warming, ozone depletion, pollution and land degradation, which is why sustainable development is needed.

questions.question: Explain the three stages of resource planning in India.
answer_steps: Identification and inventory of resources across the regions of the country: surveying, mapping and qualitative and quantitative estimation.
Evolving a planning structure endowed with appropriate technology, skill and institutional set-up for implementing the plans.
Matching the resource development plans with the overall national development plans.

questions.question: Suggest three ways to solve the problem of land degradation.
answer_steps: Afforestation, proper management of grazing and control on overgrazing.
Planting shelter belts and stabilising sand dunes by growing thorny bushes.
Proper management of wastelands, control of mining, and proper treatment and disposal of industrial effluents.

questions.question: Describe three features of laterite soil.
answer_steps: It develops under high temperature and heavy rainfall, as a result of intense leaching.
It is low in humus because decomposers like bacteria are destroyed by high temperature.
With manures and conservation methods it supports tea and coffee; red laterite in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala suits cashew nut.

questions.question: Describe the features and distribution of black soil and alluvial soil in India.
answer_steps: Alluvial soil covers the northern plains, deposited by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; it extends to Rajasthan and Gujarat and the eastern coast deltas.

Alluvial soil consists of sand, silt and clay, is rich in potash, phosphoric acid and lime, and is divided into bangar (old) and khadar (new, more fertile); it suits sugarcane, paddy, wheat and pulses.
Black (regur) soil is formed from the basalt lava of the Deccan trap and covers Maharashtra, Saurashtra, Malwa, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and the Godavari and Krishna valleys.
Black soil is clayey and holds moisture; it is rich in calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime but poor in phosphorus; it is ideal for cotton.
Black soil develops deep cracks in hot weather, which aerate it, and turns sticky when wet, so it must be tilled after the first shower or in the pre-monsoon period.

questions.question: What is soil erosion? Explain its causes and four methods of soil conservation.
answer_steps: Soil erosion is the denudation of the soil cover and its washing down; human activities upset the balance between soil formation and erosion.
Causes: deforestation, overgrazing, construction, mining and defective farming such as ploughing up and down the slope; natural agents are water, wind and glaciers.
Running water makes gullies and bad land (ravines in the Chambal basin); water also causes sheet erosion, and wind blows away loose soil.
Contour ploughing and terrace cultivation (as in the western and central Himalayas) slow down water on slopes.
Strip cropping and shelter belts break the force of wind; shelter belts have stabilised sand dunes in western India.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"In June 1992, more than 100 heads of states met in Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, for the first International Earth Summit. The Summit was convened for addressing urgent problems of environmental protection and socio-economic development at the global level."* (NCERT)

(i) Why was the Earth Summit convened? (1)

(ii) Name the agenda adopted at the summit. (1)

(iii) Explain the main objective of this agenda and what it expects from local governments. (2)
answer_steps: (i) To address urgent problems of environmental protection and socio-economic development at the global level.
(ii) Agenda 21.

(iii) It aims to combat environmental damage, poverty and disease through global co-operation on common interests, mutual needs and shared responsibilities; every local government should draw up its own local Agenda 21.

questions.question:
Read the source and answer the questions.

*"Black soil is made up of extremely fine i.e. clayey material. It is well-known for its capacity to hold moisture. In addition, it is rich in soil nutrients, such as calcium carbonate, magnesium, potash and lime. This soil is generally poor in phosphoric contents. It develops deep cracks during hot weather, which helps in the proper aeration of the soil."* (NCERT)

(i) Which crop is black soil best suited for? (1)

(ii) Which nutrient is black soil poor in? (1)

(iii) Why must black soil be tilled immediately after the first shower or during the pre-monsoon period? Give one more feature. (2)
answer_steps: (i) Cotton.
(ii) Phosphoric content.
(iii) It becomes sticky when wet and is difficult to work on, so it is tilled when just moist; it also develops deep cracks in hot weather, which help aeration.
